title: Propulsion of magnetic domain walls via elastic damping in magnetostrictive materials
authors: Miguel Moreno, Rocio Yanes, Luis Lopez-Diaz
abstract: The interaction between magnetic and elastic degrees of freedom is increasingly central to advanced spintronics technology. In magnetostrictive materials, a moving domain wall carries a localized elastic deformation. Here, we investigate these elastic deformations and their back-action on field-driven domain wall dynamics using a fully coupled micromagnetic-elastodynamic framework and an analytical collective coordinates model. We show that mechanical damping acts as a non-magnetic dissipation channel, extracting energy from the magnetic texture and sustaining translational domain wall motion even in the complete absence of intrinsic Gilbert damping ($α=0$). Specifically, elastic damping impacts domain wall dynamics in a manner equivalent to magnetic losses, allowing us to map it onto an effective magnetoelastic contribution to the Gilbert damping parameter, $α_\text{me}$. We calculate the localized stress tensor profiles co-moving with the domain wall and show that mechanical dissipation breaks their spatial symmetry. Using our collective coordinates model, we demonstrate that these asymmetric stress profiles-specifically the localized stress gradients across the wall core-exert direct propelling forces that balance field-induced magnetic precession, enabling steady-state motion. Overall, these findings reveal a fundamental energy transfer and relaxation mechanism between magnetic and elastic subsystems, providing valuable insights for controlling magnetic texture dynamics via strain engineering and mechanical damping design in acoustic spintronic devices.
summary: This paper analyzes the propulsion of magnetic domain walls in magnetostrictive materials by coupling micromagnetics with elastodynamics. It demonstrates that mechanical damping acts as a crucial, non-magnetic energy sink, enabling steady-state DW motion even when intrinsic magnetic damping is absent. This reveals a fundamental energy exchange mechanism vital for designing advanced acoustic spintronic devices.
main_problem: The study investigates how elastic damping in magnetostrictive materials propels magnetic domain walls (DWs) by providing a non-magnetic energy dissipation channel.
main_result: Mechanical damping sustains DW motion even when intrinsic Gilbert damping is zero, and the resulting asymmetric stress gradients exert direct propelling forces balancing field-induced precession.
method: The research employs a fully coupled micromagnetic-elastodynamic framework, supplemented by an analytical 1D collective coordinates model for simplification.
model_or_system: The system models a perpendicularly magnetized magnetostrictive ferromagnet (e.g., in an ultrathin nanowire) where magnetization dynamics (LLG equation) are coupled to mechanical displacement (elastodynamic wave equation) via magnetoelastic interactions.
key_observables: Localized stress tensor profiles ($\sigma_{xx}, \sigma_{xy}, \sigma_{xz}$), DW velocity ($v_{dw}$), and the effective magnetoelastic damping parameter ($\alpha_{me}$).
important_parameters: Intrinsic Gilbert damping ($\alpha$), elastic damping constant ($\eta$), magnetostriction constants ($\lambda_{100}, \lambda_{111}$), and applied magnetic field ($B_z$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on a 1D reduction of the full 3D problem, assuming transverse mechanical modes are frozen or that the dynamics are subsonic.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the DW position, velocity vs. field, and profiles of magnetization, mechanical displacement, and strain under various damping conditions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the coupled governing equations (LLG and elastodynamics) to solving the static equilibrium profiles, and finally analyzing the dynamic regimes, particularly focusing on the steady-state balance equations derived from the collective coordinates model.
why_interesting: While focused on classical condensed matter physics, the concept of energy dissipation channels (mechanical vs. magnetic) and the mapping of one dissipation mechanism onto an effective damping parameter ($\alpha_{me}$) is highly relevant to understanding energy loss in quantum-limited spintronic devices.
